title: West Sikkim homestays: villages, prices and what to ask
meta_description: Homestays in West and South Sikkim: Uttarey, Hee Bermiok, Kaluk, Dentam, Okhrey, Kewzing, Yuksom and Khecheopalri, with 2025–26 prices and booking questions.
summary: A West Sikkim homestay costs about ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with dinner and breakfast, in a family house in a farming village. The best villages are Uttarey, Hee Bermiok, Kaluk, Dentam, Okhrey, Kewzing, Yuksom and Khecheopalri. Book by phone, confirm meals, heating and road access, and expect simple, warm rooms.

sections.heading: How a Sikkim village homestay works
paras: A homestay here is usually two to five guest rooms in, or beside, a farming family's house. The family cooks for you, often in the same kitchen they use themselves, and your rate nearly always includes dinner and breakfast. Sikkim Tourism registers rural homestays and has promoted them for years as a way to keep tourist money in villages, so in the west and south you will find them in places that have no hotel at all.

What you get is not luxury but closeness. Dinner is dal, rice, a seasonal vegetable, perhaps gundruk or nettle soup and local chicken, with dalle khursani chilli on the side. Breakfast might be puri, sel roti or Tibetan bread with eggs. You hear the cows in the morning, see cardamom drying and learn how a ridge village really runs. For families on a budget and for travellers who want to talk to the people who live here, it is the best value in the region.

A typical day runs on farm time. Tea comes at about 6 am, often with the first light on Kanchenjunga, and breakfast at 8. Hosts are usually happy to send a son, daughter or neighbour to walk you to a waterfall, a monastery or the cardamom fields, and to arrange the next morning's jeep seat. Evenings are early: by 9 pm most villages are dark and silent, so bring a book, a torch and a power bank.

sections.heading: Villages worth a booking
paras: We describe these villages rather than name individual houses, because family homestays open, close and change hands often. The one exception is Yangsum Heritage Farm at Rinchenpong, a long-running family farmstay we are confident about.
list: Uttarey: about 2,000 m near the Nepal border, below the Singalila ridge. Homestays line the village; walks to the Mainebas waterfall and towards Chewabhanjyang. Cold from November to February.
Hee Bermiok: a farming village on the Pelling to Dentam side, with cardamom, maize and a wide view of Kanchenjunga across the Rangeet valley. Quiet and good for a two-night pause.
Kaluk and Rinchenpong: neighbouring villages in Soreng district at about 1,600–1,700 m, known for orange and cardamom farms and clear dawn views. Yangsum Heritage Farm is here.
Dentam: a valley of rice terraces and farmland at about 1,500 m, on the road to Uttarey and the Singshore Bridge. Warmer than the ridges, so good in winter.
Okhrey: below Hilley, the base for the walk into Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary. Book here in March and April for the bloom.
Kewzing: near Ravangla in South Sikkim, a Bhutia village known for its homestay cluster and for the Bon monastery at Yungdrung Kundrakling.
Yuksom: the trailhead for Goecha La, with family guesthouses and homestays around the bazaar and fields. Good before or after a trek.
Khecheopalri: the village and gompa above the sacred lake, with a few simple homestays. Very quiet after dark.

sections.heading: Matching the village to your trip
paras: The villages differ more than the brochures suggest, mainly by height, by how far they are from a jeep route and by what lies at the end of a walk. A rough rule: the higher the village, the clearer and colder the mornings, and the fewer the jeeps. Pair one ridge village with one valley village and you see both sides of farm life here, the cardamom and paddy below and the forest and high pastures above.
list: First trip with children: Kaluk or Rinchenpong, on a sealed road with short walks and big views.
Trekkers: Yuksom before Goecha La or Dzongri, Okhrey before Barsey.
Couples on a budget: Hee Bermiok or Dentam for two quiet nights between Pelling and Uttarey.
Monastery travellers: Khecheopalri for the lake at dawn, Kewzing for the Bon monastery and Ravangla's sites.
Winter visitors: Dentam and Kaluk, which stay warmer than Uttarey and Okhrey.

sections.heading: What is included and what it costs
paras: Prices below are indicative for 2025–26, per person per night on twin sharing unless stated. They rise by ₹200–500 around Durga Puja, Diwali and Christmas, and fall in the monsoon. Children under about eight often stay free or at half rate; ask.

list: Dinner is usually at about 7–8 pm, often with the family; tell them in advance if you are vegetarian, vegan or Jain.
Tea on arrival and in the morning is normally free. Beer and local chhang or tongba, where offered, are extra.
Most families take cash or UPI, but village network is weak, so carry enough cash for your stay.

sections.heading: Questions to ask before you book
paras: Most bookings in these villages are by phone or WhatsApp, often through a relative in Pelling or Gangtok. That works well if you ask the right things up front and get the answers in writing.
list: Is the rate per person or per room, and does it include dinner and breakfast?
Is the toilet attached or shared, Western or Indian style, and is there hot water all day?
Can a car reach the door, or is there a walk with luggage? How long, and is it steep?
Which mobile network works in the house, and is there Wi-Fi when the power is on?
Is there heating or an electric blanket from November to February?
Can you arrange a car or a seat in the morning jeep for onward travel, and at what price?
Is the homestay registered with Sikkim Tourism? Registered houses are inspected and listed.
What is the advance and the cancellation rule if a landslide blocks the road?

sections.heading: Monsoon and winter at a homestay
paras: From June to September rain is heavy and landslides cut village roads for hours or days at a time. Rates drop and the farms are green, but views of Kanchenjunga are rare and leeches are common on paths. If you go, keep a free day in your plan, choose a village on a main road such as Dentam or Yuksom, and check current status before you travel.

December to February is dry and clear, with the best mountain views of the year, but higher villages are cold. Uttarey, Okhrey and Kewzing can drop below zero at night, and most houses have no central heating. Pack thermals, a hat and woollen socks, ask for an electric blanket or extra quilt, and drink water even when you do not feel thirsty. Dentam and the lower fields around Hee Bermiok stay a few degrees warmer.

sections.heading: Being a good guest
paras: A homestay works because a family opens its home, so the rules are those of any house. Take your shoes off at the door if the family does. Eat what is cooked or say early what you cannot eat. Ask before photographing family members, prayer rooms or children. Switch off lights and the geyser when you leave the room, because power is precious. Carry your plastic back to town; village waste systems are small. And if you liked the stay, tell others by name and leave a short note in the visitors' book, which helps them more than any rating site.

Tipping is not expected, but a few hundred rupees for the person who cooked or guided you is always appreciated. If you are staying with a Lepcha, Limboo or Bhutia family, ask about their festivals, food and language; most hosts enjoy explaining, and you will leave knowing far more than any guidebook can tell you.

faqs.q: How much does a homestay cost in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Indicatively ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night on twin sharing, including dinner and breakfast, in 2025–26. Lunch adds ₹150–250. Rooms with an attached Western toilet or a big view can cost a few hundred rupees more, and rates rise around Durga Puja, Diwali and Christmas. Families with small children can often negotiate a lower rate.

faqs.q: Which is the best homestay village near Pelling?
faqs.a: Hee Bermiok and Dentam are the closest farming villages, 1–1.5 hours from Pelling, with cardamom fields and mountain views. Uttarey, about 30 km beyond via Dentam, is higher and colder, near the Nepal border. Kaluk and Rinchenpong, about 2 hours away, give the clearest dawn views of Kanchenjunga. Choose by season: lower villages in winter, higher in spring.

faqs.q: How do I book a homestay in a Sikkim village?
faqs.a: Usually by phone or WhatsApp, either directly with the family or through a relative or agent in Pelling, Gangtok or Siliguri. Ask for the rate per person, what meals are included, toilet type and car access, and get the answers in writing. Many ask for a small advance by UPI. Sikkim Tourism also lists registered homestays.

faqs.q: Do homestays in Sikkim have hot water and Western toilets?
faqs.a: Most newer rooms do, with a geyser or solar heater and an attached Western toilet. Older houses may have a shared bathroom or bring hot water in a bucket from the kitchen. Power cuts are common in villages, especially in the monsoon. If either matters to you, ask before booking rather than on arrival.

faqs.q: Are homestays safe for women travelling alone?
faqs.a: In our experience the family homestays of West and South Sikkim are among the safest places to stay in the region, because you are living with a family rather than in an empty hotel. Book a registered homestay, share your plans with someone at home, and arrive before dark, since village roads are unlit and jeeps stop running by late afternoon.

faqs.q: Can I visit a homestay village in the monsoon?
faqs.a: You can, but plan for disruption. From June to September heavy rain causes landslides that block village roads, sometimes for a day or more, and views are mostly in cloud. Rates are lower and farms are green. Pick a village on a main road, keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it cold in West Sikkim homestays in winter?
faqs.a: Yes, in the higher villages. Uttarey, Okhrey and Kewzing can drop below 0 °C at night in December and January, and houses rarely have central heating. Lower villages such as Dentam stay a few degrees warmer. Bring thermals, a warm hat and socks, and ask your host for an electric blanket or an extra quilt.

faqs.q: What food is served at a Sikkim homestay?
faqs.a: Home cooking: rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable, often gundruk or nettle soup, ferns in spring, and local chicken or eggs, with dalle khursani chilli on the side. Breakfast might be sel roti, puri or Tibetan bread. Many families make chhang, a millet beer served in a bamboo tongba. Tell them in advance about vegetarian or other needs.

faqs.q: Do I need cash for homestays in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes, carry enough for your whole stay plus a margin. Many families accept UPI, but mobile data in villages is often too weak for payments to go through. The nearest ATMs are in towns such as Gyalshing, Pelling, Jorethang and Ravangla, and they sometimes run dry on long weekends, so draw cash before you head out.
